tip: Shop staff address you as 손님 (sonnim), literally 'guest' – it doubles as the polite 'sir/ma'am', so no name is needed.
물어봐요 (mureobwayo) stacks 보다 (boda = see) onto asking: ask 'and see' what happens. Korean adds 보다 to a verb to mean 'give it a try'.
살 거예요 (sal geoyeyo) here comes from 사다 (sada = buy), but 살다 (salda = live) makes the identical future form – only context tells you whether someone will buy or live.
입어 볼 거예요 (ibeo bol geoyeyo) is literally 'I'll wear it and see' – tacking 보다 (boda = see) onto a verb is how Korean says you're trying something out.
다음 달 (daeum dal = next month) uses 달 (dal), the same word as 'moon' – Korean has one word for both, a leftover from moon-based months.
남동생 (namdongsaeng) splits into 남 (nam = male) + 동생 (dongsaeng = younger sibling). Swap in 여 (yeo = female) and you get 여동생 (yeodongsaeng), a younger sister.
Korean pins down the exact family branch: 이모는 (imo-neun) tells you this aunt is on Mom's side. Dad's sister is a different word entirely – 고모 (gomo).
사촌 (sachon) literally means 'four degrees' – Korean counts kinship in steps, and a cousin is exactly four steps away through the grandparents.
결혼했어요 (gyeolhonhaesseoyo) is past tense, 'got married', but it's how Korean says someone IS married – the wedding happened, so the state holds.
Only men say 형 (hyeong) for 'older brother', so 형은 (hyeong-eun) quietly reveals the speaker is male – a woman would say 오빠 (oppa) instead.
키가 커요 (ki-ga keoyo) is literally 'height is big' – Korean talks about your 키 (ki = height) being big or small, not about you being tall or short.
써요 (sseoyo) is from 쓰다 (sseuda), the 'wear' verb for the head area – glasses, hats, masks. Korean chooses its wear-verb by body part.
얼굴이 작아요 (eolgur-i jagayo = 'the face is small') is a compliment – a small face is a Korean beauty ideal, so this is praise for the actor.
마음 (maeum) means heart and mind at once, so 마음이 따뜻해요 (maeum-i ttatteuthaeyo) praises someone's whole inner self as warm, not just their feelings.
닮았어요 (dalmasseoyo) is past tense for a present fact – Korean treats resemblance as settled long ago: you took after Dad once, and it stuck.
그분 (geubun), the respectful 'that person', pulls the verb up with it: 계세요 (gyeseyo) is the honorific 'is (somewhere)', replacing plain 있어요 (isseoyo).
스물 (seumul = twenty) shrinks to 스무 (seumu) before a counter: 스무 살 (seumu sal = twenty years). Korean numbers slim down to count, like 하나 (hana) becoming 한 (han).
나이가 많아요 (nai-ga manayo) is literally 'age is many' – Korean stacks up years instead of calling someone old, and it works for dogs too.
나이가 어떻게 돼요? (nai-ga eotteoke dwaeyo?) is the soft way to ask an age, roughly 'how does your age turn out?' – 몇 살이에요? (myeot sarieyo?) is the blunt version, fine for kids.
축하해요 (chukahaeyo = I congratulate) attaches to any occasion word: 생일 축하해요 (saengil chukahaeyo) is 'birthday + congratulations'. Swap in any occasion, keep the ending.
처음 뵙겠습니다 (cheoeum boepgetseumnida) is the set formal line for a first meeting – literally 'I meet you for the first time' – so it's never used twice with the same person.
이쪽은 (ijjog-eun) introduces a person as 'this side is...' – pointing at a direction rather than the person is the polite Korean way to introduce someone.
이분 (ibun), the respectful 'this person', lifts the verb ending too: 어머니세요 (eomeoni-seyo), not plain 어머니예요 (eomeoni-yeyo) – respected subjects take -세요 (-seyo).
어디에서 왔어요? (eodieseo wasseoyo?) is literally 'where did you come from?' – Korean asks about origin in the past tense, as a completed journey.
잘 지내요? (jal jinaeyo?) is literally 'are you getting along well?' – 지내다 (jinaeda) means to spend your days, so you're asking how life is passing.
마셔요 (masyeoyo) can be a statement, a question, or 'let's drink' – one polite form covers all three. 같이 (gachi = together) is the clue this one is an invitation.
로 (ro) marks your means of transport: 지하철로 (jihacheol-lo) = by subway. It works for any vehicle – 버스로 (beoseu-ro = by bus), 차로 (cha-ro = by car).
갈아타요 (garatayo) is built from 갈다 (galda = change) + 타다 (tada = ride) – transferring between lines is literally 'change-riding'.
길이 막혀요 (giri makyeoyo) is literally 'the road is blocked' – Korean describes a traffic jam from the road's point of view, not the traffic's.
부터 (buteo) glues straight onto a time word: 다음 주부터 (daeum ju-buteo) = starting next week. Its endpoint partner is 까지 (kkaji = until).
우리 회사 (uri hoesa) is 'our company' even when the listener works somewhere else – 우리 (uri) covers whatever you belong to: company, school, house.
At work Koreans use title + 님 (nim): 과장님 (gwajangnim = manager + honorific). A colleague's bare name sounds rude – the title itself is the polite address.
중 (jung) after a noun means 'in the middle of it': 출장 중 (chuljang jung) = mid-business-trip. It works everywhere – 회의 중 (hoeui jung) = in a meeting.
안 돼요 (an dwaeyo) is literally 'it doesn't become' – the all-purpose Korean for 'it's not working', whether it's a computer, a plan, or a request.
께 (kke) is the honorific 'to': 부장님께 (bujangnimkke) = to the department head. With friends it's plain 한테 (hante) – same job, no deference.
할 일 (hal il) is literally 'will-do work': 할 (hal) turns 하다 (hada = do) into a label for the noun after it. Korean builds 'things to do' straight from the verb.
다녀요 (danyeoyo), from 다니다 (danida = go regularly), is how Korean says you work somewhere: 은행에 다녀요 (eunhaeng-e danyeoyo) – showing up routinely IS the job.
실 (sil) is a 'room' suffix: 회의실 (hoeuisil) = meeting room, 화장실 (hwajangsil) = bathroom. Spot the 실 and you know it's some kind of room.
후에 (hue = after) comes after its noun: 회의 후에 (hoeui hue) is literally 'meeting-after'. Korean time words trail the thing they anchor to – reversed from English.
제가 사요 (jega sayo), 'I'm buying', is the standard offer to treat – 사다 (sada = buy) covers picking up the bill, no separate 'treat' verb needed.
에 (e) can link food pairings: 치킨에 맥주 (chikin-e maekju) = chicken with beer. The combo is so beloved it compressed into one word, 치맥 (chimaek).
많아서 (manaseo) packs 'because there's a lot' into one word – the -아서 (-aseo) ending fuses the cause onto the verb, so no separate 'because' appears.
월급날 (wolgeumnal = payday) has a sound trap: it's spelled with ㅂ (b) before ㄴ (n), but ㅂ turns into ㅁ (m) there – say -mn-, never -pn-.
못 먹었어요 (mot meogeosseoyo) = couldn't eat: 못 (mot) means circumstances stopped you. 안 (an) would mean you chose to skip breakfast.
마다 (mada) sticks straight onto a noun: 주말마다 (jumal-mada) = every weekend. No extra particle needed – 마다 does 'every' all by itself.
